title: A day of patience
hook: a monk heading to a rough place calls the people who insult him good
tomorrow: is a kind lie ever the right thing to say?

segments.voice: Yesterday Prince Canda pleaded gently with the father who'd turned on him. Patient under wrong. Today, a monk who takes it further, and it sounds strange at first.

The everyday complaints are small: the bus, the weather, the coworker who replies all. One discourse has a monk who seems to have run out of complaints entirely, and his reason is odd. His name is Punna, and he wants to go and live in Sunaparanta, where, the Buddha warns him, the people are fierce and rough. What if they insult you? Then, Punna says, I'll think: how good these people are. They didn't hit me.
screen: `THE BUS. THE WEATHER. REPLY ALL.` → `A MONK WITH NO COMPLAINTS.` → `HOW GOOD. THEY DIDN'T HIT ME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha presses. And if they hit you? Then I'll think, how good they are, they didn't throw stones. And stones? They didn't use a stick. A stick? They didn't use a knife. The puzzle is why this isn't just denial. Punna isn't pretending the insult is nice. He sees it exactly, an insult, and then he sees what it isn't. Every rough thing that comes, he sets beside something worse that didn't. That's patience as a habit of mind, and it starves complaint at the root. A complaint says: this shouldn't be happening to me. Punna says: this is happening, it could be worse, and I can bear it. The Buddha's reply is approval. With such self-control and calm, he says, you'll be able to live there. The discourse says Punna went, and people there took up the teaching through him. So a day without complaints isn't a day without problems. It's a day of naming them plainly, without the extra line that says the world owes you better.
screen: `THEY DIDN'T HIT ME.` · `NOT DENIAL: SEEING IT EXACTLY.` · `A COMPLAINT SAYS: NOT TO ME.` · `NAME IT, DROP THE EXTRA LINE.` · then, large: `NO COMPLAINTS.`

segments.voice: Get up and walk slowly for about a minute, around the room or down a hall. Each time a small complaint shows up, my feet, the cold, the noise, name it plainly and add Punna's turn: and it could be worse. Then settle back down for the rest of the sit.
A day of patience: a day of naming what's hard plainly, without the complaint on top.
Here's your line: no complaints, which still leaves room for problems, just not the extra grumble. See you then.

screen: `DAY 1563 COUNTS.` → `THE TEN PERFECTIONS · DAY 18 OF 30.` → `TOMORROW: IS A KIND LIE EVER THE RIGHT THING TO SAY?`

howItsDone: The Punnovada Sutta is often taught as a model of patience, and some Buddhists take up a day or a week of no complaining as a practice of khanti.

discourse.meaning: a recorded talk of the Buddha, a sutta

sources.ref: MN 145, Punnovada Sutta (also SN 35.88): Punna and the people of Sunaparanta

notes: Puzzle shape: the odd detail is a monk calling those who insult him good; the answer is that he sees the insult exactly and sets it beside what didn't happen.

MN 145 paraphrased. The sutta's last step (being killed) is left out on purpose; the voice stops at the knife. The detail that Punna established lay followers there is given without the sutta's number. Confirm.
Day 1401 (y4) and y2 417-419 used Vedehika and the simile of the saw for patience; this day uses Punna instead.
